summary: Defines MIB objects for managing Fibre Channel over TCP/IP entities, which interconnect Fibre Channel fabrics with IP networks. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: A control panel for gadgets that link storage networks across the ordinary internet.

subtitle: The SNMP management objects for devices that carry Fibre Channel traffic over TCP/IP.

tldr.problem: Fibre Channel over TCP/IP (FCIP) devices join Fibre Channel fabrics across IP networks, but operators had no standard way to inspect or configure them with network management tools.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4404 defines FCIP-MGMT-MIB, an SNMP MIB module with tables for FCIP entities, links, TCP connections, dynamic and static routes, discovery domains and link error counters.
tldr.outcome: Any SNMP manager can read and configure FCIP devices in a common way, with the caveat that write access must be protected, ideally with SNMPv3.

today: RFC 4404 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2006, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the FCIP management MIB module.

sections.title: What the MIB Is For
sections.content:
RFC 4404 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing Fibre Channel over TCP/IP (FCIP) entities. FCIP entities are used to interconnect Fibre Channel (FC) fabrics with IP networks. The functional behaviour of an FCIP entity is described in RFC 3821; this memo covers only how to manage it.

Managed objects are normally accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) and are written in the Structure of Management Information, version 2 (SMIv2). The module is called FCIP-MGMT-MIB and its root object fcipMIB is the first and only version of the module, last updated on 6 February 2006.
sections.eli5: Some boxes send storage traffic through the internet. This document is the list of buttons and meters that lets someone watch and control those boxes from far away.

sections.title: The FCIP Management Model
sections.content:
A collection of FCIP entity instances, together with the matching FC entities, inside one SNMP context is called an FCIP device. The device, plus the IP network it runs on, forms a new FCIP transport network that interconnects FC fabric elements. A device can work as a stand-alone box or as part of an FC fabric element.

Each device has one or more FCIP entities. Peer entities are connected by FCIP links attached to VE_ports or B_Access. Each link endpoint contains one or more Data Engines, and each link in an entity manages one or more TCP connections. The entity uses one Data Engine per TCP connection to encapsulate and de-encapsulate FC frames and to send FCIP frames on that connection.
sections.eli5: Think of a toll bridge between two towns. The bridge house is the device, each lane is a link, and every car-counting gate on a lane is a TCP connection.

sections.title: The Tables
sections.content:
The MIB is split into tables, all placed under fcipConfig:

  • Entity instances (fcipEntityInstanceTable): one row per FCIP entity, with a name of 0 to 32 characters, its IP address type (only IPv4 and IPv6) and address, an optional extra TCP listening port, and flags for sequence-number wrap protection and PHB quality-of-service support.
  • Links (fcipLinkTable): one row per link, with the interface index, the FSPF cost, whether the local end is in E-Port or B-Port mode, and the local and remote entity addresses, identifiers and World Wide Name.
  • TCP connections (fcipTcpConnTable): local and remote ports, the default maximum receiver window and the TCP maximum segment size.
  • Dynamic routes and static routes: each maps a Fibre Channel domain ID to an FCIP link.
  • Discovery domains: groups FCIP entities under a name of up to 128 characters.

There are also three scalars: the discovery protocol in use (slpv2 or none), the device World Wide Name, and whether the TCP Selective Acknowledgement option is enabled.

The dynamic table is filled by discovery, which may use the SLPv2 protocol together with others such as Fabric Shortest Path First (FSPF). The static table is filled by the network administrator. Both can be active at once, and if a domain ID appears in both, the static entry takes precedence.

Rows are created and removed through RowStatus objects. Setting an entity's status to destroy also removes its rows from the link and TCP connection tables, and destroying a link removes its TCP connection rows.
sections.eli5: The MIB is like a set of spreadsheets: one lists the boxes, one lists the roads between them, one lists the lanes on each road, and one is a map of which road leads to which town.

sections.title: Fit With Other MIBs
sections.content:
The module deliberately leaves out objects that other MIBs already provide. TCP statistics come from the TCP group (RFC 4022), and Fibre Channel functionality comes from the Fibre Channel Management MIB (RFC 4044).

Each FCIP link should appear as a row in the ifTable with a unique ifIndex and an ifType of fcipLink (224). Because FCIP runs on top of TCP/IP, ifStackLowerLayer is always 0, and the physical address is reported as 0 since a link has only a World Wide Name. The multicast and broadcast counters are not incremented, ifLinkUpDownTrapEnable defaults to disabled, and ifPromiscuousMode and ifConnectorPresent are false. The octet counters count FCIP information in TCP streams starting with the FCIP header.
sections.eli5: This MIB does not copy meters that already exist elsewhere. It just says how to read the standard ones for these special links.

sections.title: Link Error Counters
sections.content:
The fcipLinkErrorsTable holds 12 Counter32 objects per link. Each records how often a particular error happened that caused a TCP connection to close down. Discontinuities of these counters are indicated by fcipLinkCreateTime.

They cover loss of FC synchronization, FCIP encapsulation errors (improper header, format or length), missing or mismatched Special Frame responses, invalid connection nonces, duplicate Special Frames, invalid destination WWNs, FC Keep Alive timeouts, frames discarded for an expired SNTP timestamp, TCP connections closed for too many errors or too many dropped packets, and Security Association parameter mismatches.
sections.eli5: These are tally marks. Every time something goes wrong on a link, the matching counter goes up by one, so an operator can see what keeps breaking.

sections.title: Conformance Groups
sections.content:
The compliance statement makes six groups mandatory: the scalar group, entity instances, links, TCP connections, discovery domains and link errors. The dynamic route and static route groups are mandatory only for systems that do not have these objects in another FC MIB, though they may be implemented anyway.

Implementations only need to support IPv4 and IPv6 address types. The address size is four octets for IPv4 and sixteen for IPv6.
sections.eli5: A box must show the main meters to claim it follows the rules. The route maps are only needed if the box does not already show them somewhere else.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Objects with read-write or read-create access can be sensitive. Write access to fcipDiscoveryDomainName and fcipEntityAddress can cause a loss of reachability to parts of the Fibre Channel fabric, and write access to fcipStaticRouteStatus can create incorrect routes to remote devices.

Some readable objects expose identification and topology, such as the device and remote WWNs, entity names and addresses, discovery domain names and route information. Versions of SNMP before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, and even a secure network such as one using IPsec does not control who may read or change these objects. The RFC says implementers RECOMMENDED to consider SNMPv3 security, and deploying older SNMP versions is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: If a stranger could turn the dials, they could send your storage traffic the wrong way. So only trusted people should get the keys, and the keys should be strong ones.
